headline: UK start-up Aegiq and the University of Sheffield published a design for a light-based quantum computer that they calculate can tolerate far more lost light than earlier designs.
score_reason: Pool score 5 lowered by 1: the paper appeared on 8 Oct and was covered on 9 Oct, and the '4x' headline compares against a single earlier figure for a calculated, not built, design.
importance_line: A design that survives more lost light would make light-based quantum computers easier to build, which matters to researchers and later to fields like drug and materials design, but it is a calculation from one start-up with no machine shown and it relies on photon sources that cannot yet be made in the quantity needed.
summary: Tech Times reports that Aegiq, a Sheffield quantum start-up, and the University of Sheffield published a peer-reviewed paper on 8 Oct 2026 in Quantum Science and Technology describing QGATE, a design for a quantum computer that uses photons (particles of light) as its qubits, the basic units of quantum information. The authors calculate that errors can still be corrected when 10.4% or 26% of photons are lost, depending on the set-up, against a best earlier published figure of 6.4% (Quandela, 2024), but these are theoretical results that assume a source of single photons on demand that has not yet been shown in the quantity needed.
notes: Read the full Tech Times text. Headline's '4x ... any rival' not repeated; it compares the higher 25.98% figure with one earlier figure (6.4%). Thresholds are calculated, not measured on hardware. Tech Times wrote its own long report from the paper (DOI 10.1088/2058-9565/aea970 as given by the article); the paper itself was not opened.
